story_text.value:
Mobile carriers have long supported email-to-SMS functionality, but in the United States, the big three (Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T) have deprecated these services. So a crop of commercial email-to-SMS services have sprung up, and one of my SaaS tools is exactly that.

But because SMS is so regulated now, and the 10DLC process is such a pain, and because I wanted to support international numbers, I embarked on making email-to-iMessage work, and I finally figured it out.

Try it now: Send an email to your-number@i.text.email.

If you have a non-U.S., non-Canadian number, be sure to include the country code.

U.S. Example: 2125551234@i.text.email U.K. Example: 447700900000@i.text.email India Example: 919876543210@i.text.email

Whatever you do, don't forget the "i"!

Website: https://text.email

story_text.value:
I built BScaff, a CLI tool for saving and reusing project structures, templates, files, and text snippets. It can serve as a URL bookmark tool as well.

It started with project scaffolding, but I wanted something more general-purpose: a tool that could save almost any reusable starting point and bring it back whenever needed. For each language, I had a specific way of structuring projects that I have refined over years, but I could not find any tool which can quickly help to generate such scaffolding quickly. Copier and Cookiecutter exists but they depend on templates, and I didn't want to create templates for such tasks. One more use-case I had was when I used AI chatbots who suggest some project structure, and I want to quickly create that. So I wanted something offline which can quickly help me save and recreate file trees. Then I added snippets to it too, but I mostly use it for notes taking personally.

Some things you can do with it:

* Save Git repository templates locally and use them offline whenever you need to create a new project

* Create reusable templates from existing directories

* Save and recreate directory structures by copying ASCII file trees and the tool will read it from clipboard and recreate it (or save it for later)

* Save collections of files and generate them again in another directory

* Save text snippets and either copy them to the clipboard or generate files from them

The idea is to avoid repeatedly recreating the same boilerplate, directory structures, configuration files, etc. And you can use it as a note-taking app as well with snippets. It has templates support as well with Jinja-based variable replacement. Template updates are supported, but project updates are not yet implemented, have planned it for future.

It is written in TypeScript, runs on Node.js, and is available on npm.

GitHub: https://github.com/akashnag/bscaff

Install: npm install -g @akashnag/bscaff

Feedback, feature suggestions ( I already have a big backlog though :P ), and contributions are welcome!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built Merlin to let you use your own Claude Code and Codex subscription from Slack, Linear, and GitHub.

There is a desktop app for macOS and Windows, and a CLI daemon for Linux. When someone mentions Merlin in a Slack thread or Linear issue comment, the task runs on that team member's machine, using their own Claude Code or Codex runtime, and progress and results come back to the original thread. Teammates can steer the agent mid-run. Merlin also has schedules, shared skills, and memory.

I know you've probably heard about Claude Tag. Merlin is similar to that but also different. The model usage goes to the Claude Code or Codex subscription instead of API bill, and you can use Merlin across different surfaces to streamline workflow instead of just in Slack (Linear's agent session works particularly well with Merlin. You can just leverage Linear as your control panel for agentic work using Merlin). Merlin also runs on your local machines, which means that you can use your local context including MCPs, skills and local files instead of in a cloud sandbox.

Merlin does not upload your working directory, and provider credentials stay on the device. The request and the context it needs pass through Merlin. Runtimes start private, and an owner can make one public so teammates, including non-engineers, can use it.

But there're also some limits, and we'll probably deal with them in future updates: - An offline or sleeping machine can't take work. The same issue as OpenClaw. But if you have a mac mini or ec2 setup it should be fine. - Linux is CLI only. We may later add desktop for Linux. - While runtime delegation isn't a problem for now, we're still working on how to make the best use of each team member's local runtime and let them work together cohesively.

We've been internally using Merlin for quite some time. It really helps when you're trying to add some AI juice to the conversation or just delegate things to your agents. I think it reduces the friction of having to do the copying & pasting and switch to another app to ask for AI's input when you're having a discussion in a collaborative environment like Slack or Linear. It's really the fastest way from intent to execution.

Pricing: free for up to 5 active users and 1,000 requests/month. We think this should get small teams started and get real value from it. Team is $59/mo and Scale is $99/mo, with a 14-day Team trial and no credit card required.

I'm here all day to answer questions, and I'd especially like to hear whether non-engineers on your team would actually use this.

story_text.value:
I built this tool with a lot of help from Claude, for both the code and the research, so I hope you'll take that into account.

Once you've pasted in a tweet draft, you get a score with suggested improvements for the hook, specificity, answerability, and bait phrases for your draft, as well as a compare feature for two drafts. It's free and doesn't require an account.

The checklist is based on open sourced ranking code from X themselves (xai-org/x-algorithm), some research studies, and some published data from Buffer. Claude helped me comb through these resources and I turned them into these rules. I haven't tested the score against tweet performance, so I can't claim it has any bearing on virality, but I have applied the rules to drafts to check them.

It's free and doesn't require an account; the big box on the right is an ad for my other project, TweetBrain, a tweet drafting tool that's in development. It's completely separate from this one, and I'm doing this mostly as a self-reminder to promote it, since it's my thing and I should tell people about it myself.

Let me know what rules seem wrong to you, or if something like this is useful at all.

story_text.value:
The idea came to me while I was watching a livestream with Antirez and mr RIP, one of the first streams they did together.
I thought Antirez might be right when he said that once AI agents moved beyond the terminal, we would reach a whole new level. So I decided to create "Veduta", which is basically Hermes/OpenClaw but with a UI.
What exactly is the advantage? It could track everything for you and give you visual feedback without you actually having to ask the same questions again, because all the information is stored inside the daemon running on the server.
Instead of having something that just runs, you have something that delivers "sheets with written reports that you can consult at any time." This translates into saving tokens and accessing information faster, while also keeping everything organized.
I don't know if you'll appreciate this open-source project, but feel free to leave any kind of feedback. It's always welcome! :)
Thanks, everyone!

story_text.value:
Approximatr uses your built-in ability to gauge sizes, distances, alignments, angles etc to see how good your eyes are!

I've been building this for a few months, and it's been fun discovering what types of puzzles humans are good at, and terrible at - for example we're pretty good at finding the middle of something, and terrible at comparing geometric areas. It's remarkable sometimes how I'll prototype a new puzzle, and find it absolutely impossible to achieve a good result reliably even with practice, or find I'll be able to get bang-on 100% of the time - discovering the balance between the two has been quite a journey.

title.value: Show HN: Approximatr: The daily game of spatial intuition

story_text.value:
Proposal specification: https://x-ryl669.github.io/codepill/

I've got frustrated of selecting the right licenses in many of my projects, because of the subtle differences in all of them and the large incompatibilities while mixing them. Also, I often find that some part of a document should be more restricted that the rest (think of a documentation you want in public domain citing GPLv3 code, or a GPLv3 code citing restricted standard text). Also, this scheme should be able to merge both "textual" licenses with "artistic" licenses like CC.

Hence I'm proposing a new scheme that clearly specifies what "rights" you're reserving for what part of a document, media, opus, speech. It's composable, it's simple to use for both humans and machine, it allows to deny machine processing (under the jurisdictions that do protect citizens against those).

I'm asking for feedback for this idea, is there something that you'd like to protect that I've forgotten, or do you find it convenient to use and understand ?

story_text.value:
Hi Hacker News! I'm Tim, and I made y'all some Pasta. :)

Others have New Year's resolutions to get fit, mine's to build an app in hopes of getting fit.

Fun fact, I built something like this over 10 years ago but never released it. Co-founder issues, if you must know. I called it Träna Fit, träna being the Swedish word for train. I remember hiring a voice actor on Fiverr to record every rep count.

Fast forward to today and the models are good enough to do much of this, and more. Pasta is a personal trainer app for iPhone. You ask for a workout by voice or text, Apple's Foundation Models build it, and a small voice model running on the phone (Kokoro-82M) guides you as you train.

When it comes to planning and generation, I have to admit it still has plenty of room for improvement. I grade what it writes with evals. My favorite catch so far: I asked for a 500 kg deadlift for 100 reps, and the model built it, no questions asked. I'm hoping to make the evals better as I get more feedback on what's working and what's not. Over time, I'd like it to come as close as possible to what a certified personal trainer would build for you based on your goals and needs.

I also realize that getting fit and working out isn't solely about knowing what to do. There's also the motivation + accountability part, and I do have some ideas on the roadmap that I'll share later. And I swear, it's not gamifying your health and fitness results.

You'll need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence on iOS 27, and it's free for 7 days. Give it a try. I'd love to know what you ask it for first, and whether you'd do the workout it builds.

title.value: Show HN: Train with Pasta. Workouts Powered by Apple Intelligence

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I am Alessandro Afloarei and I am so happy to show you Calendar0. Calendar0 is a calendar app for the web, plus a tray/menu bar app for macOS, Windows and Linux.

It shows Google, Outlook and iCloud calendars, lets you add events quickly, has booking links, and can record and transcribe calls.

I started it in September 2025 as a hobby project for keeping all my calendars in one place, easy to reach, and over the last months I added so many new features to it.

A few details that might be interesting:

Quick add uses a mix of chrono, Jev and Gemini. It is also capable of automatically adding guests from names.

Recording captures the mic and the system audio (no bots) and uses AssemblyAI for the transcription. Afterwards, the audio file is deleted.

There's also an MCP server, so you can connect it to Claude or ChatGPT and ask about your week or meetings.

To try it you have to sign in and connect a calendar, since it can't do much without one. It is mostly free (quick add, booking links, MCP connector). I ask for an upgrade only where I actually pay myself for the feature itself, e.g. meeting transcription.

I have so many feature ideas in mind, like connecting Linear tickets to each event and add support for tasks.

I'd love to hear your feedback on the project!

Thanks a lot, Alessandro
